title: Remember me
hookLine: Rossetti: better to forget and smile than remember and be sad
tomorrow: what did a medieval abbess mean by the green in everything?

cards: People leave instructions: the playlist for the funeral, who gets the dog, don't wear black. Rossetti wrote hers as a sonnet. It opens: "Remember me when I am gone away, Gone far away into the silent land."
Remember me, she asks, when you can no longer hold me by the hand. And then, partway through, she changes her mind.

teach.h: YET IF YOU SHOULD FORGET ME.
teach.b: "Yet if you should forget me for a while And afterwards remember, do not grieve."

teach.h: BETTER BY FAR: FORGET AND SMILE.
teach.b: And the close: "Better by far you should forget and smile Than that you should remember and be sad."
That's the teaching of the sonnet: love that asks to be remembered, and then loves you enough to release you from the asking. The one leaving cares more that you can smile than that she is kept.
Some readers hear the silent land as death, and hear Rossetti's Christian faith underneath. But the gift in the poem is plain enough for anyone: permission.
Now, review day, and the road since Whitman. The thing with feathers: hope that asks nothing. He kindly stopped: death as a courteous caller.
Tell it slant: all the truth, by a gentle road. Nobody too: a pair of the unknown. A slant of light: a hurt that leaves meaning.
A bobolink for a chorister: heaven all along. Give my heart.

how: Rossetti's Remember is read at some funerals and memorials; some people choose it ahead of time as their own wish for the ones they leave.

o: a love letter Rossetti sent before a long sea voyage
a hymn sung at Victorian funerals for young children
Rossetti's sonnet that asks to be remembered, then frees you

games.q: a sonnet that turns: tap the pairs.
p: if you forget for a while
better than remember and be sad

s: the sonnet only asks to be remembered
it turns: better forget and smile than remember and be sad.
the speaker cares more that you smile than that she is kept

games.q: your friend's grandpa once told her, 'don't spend your life sad over me.' at the lunch after his funeral she laughs, then feels guilty. what fits Rossetti?
o: her laughter honors his wish; love can release the living to smile.
she should hold back laughter to show how much she cared.
she should try to forget him quickly; memory is the problem.
games.why: Rossetti doesn't ask to be forgotten; she asks that remembering never cost a smile. the grandpa's wish is the same gift.

practice: Bring to mind someone who'd miss you if you moved far away. On a scrap of paper, write them one sentence of permission in your own words: if missing me hurts, smile instead. Keep it, or give it to them someday.

wordCard.voice: Remember me: Rossetti's sonnet that asks to be remembered, then lets go: better you forget and smile than remember and be sad.

carryVoice: For the road: forget and smile. Love that sets the other one free to be glad. A new voice tomorrow.
